## What you will learn

- Explain which Linux isolation boundaries (device cgroup, network, IPC, mount namespaces) a robot container must cross, and why each ROS problem in Docker maps to one of them.
- Pass a serial device (the Pico) or camera into a container with `--device` and the right group, and handle hot-plugging without `--privileged`.
- Show RViz/Gazebo windows from a container on native Ubuntu (X11), in WSL2 (WSLg) and on Docker Desktop for Windows.
- Choose between bridge and host networking for ROS 2, and fix the "topics are listed but no messages arrive" shared-memory trap.
- Pick the right official ROS image for amd64 vs arm64, and use the course's `labs/docker` image.

## Why it matters

Docker is how the course gives everyone the same ROS 2 Jazzy + Gazebo Harmonic stack, whatever their host OS:
[04.02 Installing ROS 2](../../04-ros2/04.02-installing-ros2.md) offers "Docker on Windows" as a path,
[03.11 CI and reproducibility](../../03-robot-software/03.11-ci-and-reproducibility.md) runs tests in the same image you develop in, and the
Jetson's Isaac ROS stack only ships as dev containers. You already know Docker for web services. Robots add three things web services never need:
**hardware devices**, **GUI windows**, and **multicast/shared-memory networking**. Each has a trap that costs days if you meet it cold,
and a tempting shortcut (`--privileged`) that hides bugs until the robot is in production.

## Concept

### A container is a process with walls

A container isn't a VM. It's a normal Linux process (on the host kernel, [FL.06](FL.06-processes-systemd.md)) placed inside several
**namespaces** and **cgroups**:

| Wall | Isolates | Robot consequence | Opening in it |
|---|---|---|---|
| mount namespace | the filesystem view | host `/dev/ttyACM0` and the X11 socket aren't visible | `--device`, `-v /tmp/.X11-unix:…` |
| **device cgroup** | which device *numbers* may be opened | even a device file you create inside can't be opened (`Operation not permitted`) | `--device`, `--device-cgroup-rule` |
| user/groups | permissions | the container user needs the device's group ID ([FL.05](FL.05-permissions-users-groups.md)) | `--group-add` |
| network namespace | interfaces, ports, multicast | DDS discovery to the Pi, mDNS | `--network host` |
| **IPC namespace** (+ `/dev/shm`) | shared memory | Fast DDS on "the same host" tries shared memory and fails silently | `--ipc host` |
| capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor | privileged syscalls | real-time scheduling, raw sockets | `--cap-add SYS_NICE`, `--ulimit rtprio=…` |

`--privileged` knocks down **all** of these walls at once. Think of each flag above as opening one specific firewall port, while
`--privileged` turns the firewall off.

### What runs where on a Windows laptop

Docker Desktop on Windows runs containers inside **its own** WSL2 VM, not inside your Ubuntu-24.04 WSL distro and not on Windows.
"Host" therefore means *that VM*: `--network host` gives you the VM's network, not your Wi-Fi card. That single fact explains most
"works on my Linux colleague's laptop, not on mine" Docker/ROS problems. For multi-machine ROS (laptop ↔ Pi), native Ubuntu or WSL2
with mirrored networking ([FL.02](FL.02-installing-ubuntu.md)) beats Docker Desktop. For single-machine simulation, CI and "try it
without installing", Docker is excellent.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "For each of these flags (--device, --group-add, --network host, --ipc host, --privileged), tell me which kernel mechanism it changes and what an attacker inside the container gains."

## Technical explanation

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Version-sensitive** (verified 2026-09 against ROS 2 Jazzy images, Docker Desktop 4.x with engine 29.7 on Windows 11 / WSL 2.6.3, Ubuntu 24.04).
> Before following these steps, check the current docs: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/host/ and https://github.com/microsoft/wslg/blob/main/samples/container/Containers.md
> AI teacher: verify against current documentation before giving instructions.

### Level 1 — Images for ROS 2 Jazzy

| Image | Arch | Contains | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ros:jazzy-ros-core` / `ros:jazzy-ros-base` | amd64 + **arm64** | ROS core / + common libs and CLI tools | the Pi, headless nodes, CI |
| `ros:jazzy-perception` | amd64 + arm64 | + image pipeline, PCL | vision nodes |
| `osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop` / `jazzy-desktop-full` | **amd64 only** | + RViz, rqt, (full: Gazebo, demos) | laptop GUI and simulation |
| course `karmel-ros:jazzy` from [`labs/docker/Dockerfile`](../../labs/docker/Dockerfile) | amd64 (arm64 with `BASE_IMAGE=ros:jazzy-ros-base`) | desktop-full + ros_gz, ros2_control, Nav2, slam_toolbox, non-root user `ros` in `dialout,video,plugdev` | the course's dev container |

Docker Hub's multi-arch manifests pick the right architecture automatically. An amd64-only image on the Pi fails with
`exec format error` ([FL.01](FL.01-why-linux.md)). The official images' entrypoint sources `/opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash` for the container's
main command.

### Level 2 — Devices

```bash
docker run --rm -it --device /dev/ttyACM0 --group-add dialout ros:jazzy-ros-base bash
```

- `--device HOST[:CONTAINER]` creates the device node inside **and** adds a device-cgroup allow rule for its major:minor.
- The node keeps its host **group ID** (20 = `dialout` on Ubuntu). A non-root container user needs `--group-add dialout` (or the numeric GID),
  or must already be in that group in the image. The course image adds its `ros` user to `dialout,video,plugdev`.
- Pass the **resolved** path: `--device "$(readlink -f /dev/serial/by-id/usb-MicroPython_…)"`. udev doesn't run inside containers,
  so no `by-id` symlinks or custom udev names exist in there.

What each wall does, verified on Docker Desktop (engine 29.7):

```text
# no --device: create a ttyACM node by hand and open it
$ docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash -c 'mknod /dev/ttyACM0 c 166 0; exec 3<>/dev/ttyACM0'
bash: line 1: /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted          ← device cgroup blocks major 166

# allow the major number: the cgroup lets it through, the (VM) kernel has no such device
$ docker run --rm --device-cgroup-rule='c 166:* rmw' ubuntu:24.04 bash -c 'mknod /dev/ttyACM0 c 166 0; exec 3<>/dev/ttyACM0'
bash: line 1: /dev/ttyACM0: No such device or address

# --device for a path that doesn't exist on the host (Pico unplugged, or Windows host without usbipd)
$ docker run --rm --device /dev/ttyACM0 ubuntu:24.04 true
docker: Error response from daemon: error gathering device information while adding custom device "/dev/ttyACM0": no such file or directory
```

**Hot-plugging.** `--device` is evaluated once at container start. If you unplug and replug the Pico, the host gets a fresh node, and the
container either still has a stale one or none. The least-privilege pattern for devices that come and go:

```bash
docker run --rm -it -v /dev:/dev --device-cgroup-rule='c 166:* rmw' --group-add dialout ros:jazzy-ros-base bash
```

This bind-mounts `/dev` (new nodes appear inside) and allows only character major 166 (USB ACM serial). Cameras are major 81 (video4linux).
Find majors with `ls -l /dev/ttyACM0` on the host.

**Devices on Windows.** Docker Desktop containers can't see Windows COM ports. Get the device into Linux first: `usbipd attach --wsl`
([FL.02](FL.02-installing-ubuntu.md)) makes it appear in WSL. For hardware work on a Windows laptop, running the driver natively in WSL is simpler than
Docker Desktop. Docker's own USB/IP feature for Desktop exists, but needs a privileged helper container.

### Level 3 — GUI windows (RViz, rqt, Gazebo)

A Linux GUI app talks to a display server through a **Unix socket**: X11 at `/tmp/.X11-unix/X0` (selected by `DISPLAY=:0`), or Wayland
at `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/$WAYLAND_DISPLAY`. The container needs the socket and the environment variable.

**Native Ubuntu 24.04 desktop** (Wayland session with XWayland, or X11):

```bash
xhost +local:                      # allow local (non-network) clients, including containers, to connect to X
docker run --rm -it -e DISPLAY -v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop ros2 run rviz2 rviz2
xhost -local:                      # revoke when done
```

**Docker Engine installed inside WSL2** (Microsoft's documented container setup for WSLg):

```bash
docker run --rm -it -v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix -v /mnt/wslg:/mnt/wslg \
  -e DISPLAY -e WAYLAND_DISPLAY -e XDG_RUNTIME_DIR -e PULSE_SERVER \
  osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop ros2 run rviz2 rviz2
```

**Docker Desktop for Windows** (commands typed in PowerShell). Docker Desktop's VM exposes the WSLg X socket at
`/run/desktop/mnt/host/wslg/.X11-unix`. Verified on this setup: `xdpyinfo` in a container reported `vendor string: Microsoft Corporation`, which
is the WSLg X server:

```powershell
docker run --rm -it -e DISPLAY=:0 -v /run/desktop/mnt/host/wslg/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop ros2 run rviz2 rviz2
```

Without the socket mount, the same container prints `xdpyinfo:  unable to open display ":0".` (or `qt.qpa.xcb: could not connect to display` from RViz).
This path relies on Docker Desktop internals and isn't covered by official ROS or Docker documentation. If it breaks after an update, use
Docker Engine inside WSL or run RViz natively in WSL. GPU acceleration: on native Linux with NVIDIA add `--gpus all` (requires the NVIDIA
Container Toolkit), and under WSL see the `/dev/dxg` example in the WSLg containers document. Without it, RViz still works on software rendering,
and Gazebo is slow.

### Level 4 — Networking and DDS

**Bridge network (default).** Each container gets its own IP on a Docker bridge (`172.17.0.0/16`, [FL.09](FL.09-networking-basics.md)).
Containers **on the same host** discover each other through DDS multicast on that bridge. Verified: a `ros2 topic pub` container and a
`ros2 topic echo` container, both on the default bridge, exchanged `data: hello`. But the bridge is NAT-ed behind the host, so **a Pi on your
Wi-Fi can't discover or reach nodes in the container**.

**Host network.** `--network host` puts the container in the host's network namespace, so DDS multicast and unicast behave like a native process.
On native Linux that's your real Wi-Fi, and cross-machine ROS works. On Docker Desktop, host networking must be enabled (Settings → Resources →
Network, Docker Desktop 4.34+). There, "host" is Docker Desktop's VM, it works at layer 4 only, and published ports are ignored. It doesn't make the
container a peer on your LAN.

**The shared-memory trap** (verified with two `ros:jazzy-ros-base` containers on Docker Desktop, 2026-09-17):

| Talker flags | Listener flags | `ros2 topic list` in listener | `ros2 topic echo --once /chatter` |
|---|---|---|---|
| (default bridge) | (default bridge) | `/chatter` | `data: hello` ✔ |
| `--network host` | `--network host` | `/chatter` (discovery works!) | **nothing, times out** ✘ |
| `--network host --ipc host` | `--network host --ipc host` | `/chatter` | `data: hello` ✔ |
| `--network host -e FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4` | same | `/chatter` | `data: hello` ✔ |

Why: with a shared network namespace, Fast DDS (Jazzy's default RMW) concludes both participants are on the same host and prefers its
**shared-memory transport**, using segments in `/dev/shm`. Separate IPC namespaces mean separate `/dev/shm`, so data never arrives, while discovery
(which also goes over UDP) looks fine. Fixes: share IPC (`--ipc host`, or the same for all ROS containers), or force UDP with
`FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4` at a small performance cost.

**`--privileged` pitfalls.** It gives the container every capability, all host devices, and no seccomp/AppArmor confinement. Root inside can mount host
disks, load kernel modules and escape trivially. For robotics it also *hides* bugs: the driver works in the privileged dev container, then fails on the
robot where the service runs as a normal user without `dialout`. Use `--device` + `--group-add`, `--device-cgroup-rule` for hotplug,
`--cap-add SYS_NICE --ulimit rtprio=90` for real-time priority, and nothing more.

## Diagram

```text
 Windows 11 laptop
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Windows: Wi-Fi card, COM ports, GPU driver, WSLg display server (RDP-based)    │
 │                                                                               │
 │  ┌─ WSL2 VM "Ubuntu-24.04" ─────────────┐   ┌─ Docker Desktop VM ───────────┐ │
 │  │ your shell, ROS 2 native (optional)  │   │ docker engine                  │ │
 │  │ /dev/ttyACM0  ← usbipd attach        │   │  ┌ container ┐  ┌ container ┐  │ │
 │  │ /mnt/wslg, /tmp/.X11-unix            │   │  │ rviz2     │  │ driver    │  │ │
 │  │ networkingMode=mirrored → LAN,       │   │  │ DISPLAY=:0│  │ --device? │  │ │
 │  │   multicast to the Pi                │   │  └─────┬─────┘  └───────────┘  │ │
 │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘   │ /run/desktop/mnt/host/wslg ◄──┘ │
 │                                             │ --network host = THIS VM,       │
 │                                             │   not the Wi-Fi LAN             │
 │                                             └────────────────────────────────┘ │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │ Wi-Fi (DDS multicast 239.255.0.1:7400+)
 ┌──────────┴───────────── Raspberry Pi 5, Ubuntu Server 24.04 (native Linux) ───┐
 │ docker run --network host --ipc host --device /dev/ttyACM0 --group-add dialout │
 │            ros:jazzy-ros-base (arm64)   → a real LAN peer, real device         │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Code

`ros-run.sh` builds a least-privilege `docker run` command for a Linux or WSL host (Docker Engine): GUI (native X11 or WSLg, auto-detected),
devices (resolving `by-id` symlinks and adding the device's group ID), and host network **with** IPC for DDS. `--dry-run` prints the command
instead of running it, so you can review what access you're granting.

`~/bin/ros-run.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ros-run.sh — start a ROS 2 Jazzy container with only the access a robot developer needs.
# Usage: ros-run.sh [--dry-run] [--gui] [--device PATH]... [--host-net] [IMAGE] [-- COMMAND...]
set -euo pipefail

image="ros:jazzy-ros-base"
dry_run=false gui=false host_net=false
args=(--rm -it -e "ROS_DOMAIN_ID=${ROS_DOMAIN_ID:-0}")
cmd=(bash)

while (( $# )); do
  case "$1" in
    --dry-run)  dry_run=true ;;
    --gui)      gui=true ;;
    --host-net) host_net=true ;;
    --device)   shift
                real=$(readlink -f "$1")                    # /dev/serial/by-id/... -> /dev/ttyACM0
                [[ -c "$real" ]] || { echo "not a character device: $1" >&2; exit 2; }
                args+=(--device "$real" --group-add "$(stat -c %g "$real")") ;;
    --)         shift; cmd=("$@"); break ;;
    -*)         echo "unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    *)          image="$1" ;;
  esac
  shift
done

if $gui; then
  if [[ -d /mnt/wslg ]]; then                                # Docker Engine inside WSL2 (WSLg)
    args+=(-v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix -v /mnt/wslg:/mnt/wslg
           -e DISPLAY -e WAYLAND_DISPLAY -e XDG_RUNTIME_DIR -e PULSE_SERVER)
  else                                                       # native Linux desktop (X11 or XWayland)
    args+=(-v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix -e "DISPLAY=${DISPLAY:?no DISPLAY set}")
    $dry_run || xhost +local: > /dev/null                    # allow local containers to use the X server
  fi
fi

if $host_net; then
  # Same network stack as the host (DDS multicast to the Pi) AND same IPC namespace,
  # otherwise Fast DDS tries shared memory with peers it cannot reach: topics appear, data never arrives.
  args+=(--network host --ipc host)
fi

if $dry_run; then
  printf '%q ' docker run "${args[@]}" "$image" "${cmd[@]}"; echo
else
  exec docker run "${args[@]}" "$image" "${cmd[@]}"
fi
```

The same choices in Compose form for a native Ubuntu host or the Pi (validated with `docker compose config`):

```yaml
# karmel-dev compose file for a native Ubuntu 24.04 host (not Docker Desktop).
services:
  sim:
    image: osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop-full        # amd64 only
    network_mode: host
    ipc: host
    environment:
      - DISPLAY=${DISPLAY}
      - ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7
    volumes:
      - /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix
      - ./ros2_ws:/home/ros/ros2_ws
    command: ros2 run rviz2 rviz2

  base-driver:
    image: ros:jazzy-ros-base                 # amd64 + arm64: same file works on the Pi
    network_mode: host
    ipc: host
    environment:
      - ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7
    devices:
      - /dev/ttyACM0:/dev/ttyACM0
    group_add:
      - dialout
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel
```

### Exercise FL.12-E1 — The shared-memory trap `[debugging]`

Hardware: none (any Docker; on Docker Desktop enable host networking first). **Predict** the result of each step, then run in two terminals:

```bash
# Terminal A
docker run --rm --name talker --network host ros:jazzy-ros-base \
  ros2 topic pub -r 5 /chatter std_msgs/msg/String '{data: hello}'
# Terminal B
docker run --rm --network host ros:jazzy-ros-base bash -c 'ros2 topic list; timeout 15 ros2 topic echo --once /chatter; echo rc=$?'
```

Hardware: `robot-base` (Pi 5 with Docker installed, Pico with MicroPython connected). Without a Pi: native Ubuntu or WSL with the Pico attached via usbipd.

1. `ros-run.sh --dry-run --device /dev/serial/by-id/usb-MicroPython_*-if00` and read the generated command.
2. Run it without `--dry-run`, then inside: `ls -l /dev/ttyACM0 && id && python3 -c "import serial; s=serial.Serial('/dev/ttyACM0',115200,timeout=1); s.write(b'\r\n'); print(s.read(64))"`
   (`python3-serial` is in the course image; in `ros:jazzy-ros-base` do `apt update && apt install -y python3-serial` first).
3. Unplug and replug the Pico, then repeat the Python line in the same container. Then restart with the hotplug pattern from Level 2 and repeat.

## Expected result

**FL.12-E1:** With `--network host` only, terminal B lists `/chatter` (plus `/parameter_events`, `/rosout`), but `echo` prints nothing and
`rc=124` (timed out): discovery worked, data didn't. With `--ipc host` on both, and with `FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4` on both, B prints
`data: hello`, `---`, `rc=0`.

**FL.12-E2:** (1) `crw-r--r-- 1 root root 166, 0 … /dev/ttyACM0` then `bash: line 1: /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted` (device cgroup).
(2) `bash: line 1: /dev/ttyACM0: No such device or address`: the cgroup allows it now, but there's no real device behind major 166 in that kernel.
(3) `docker: Error response from daemon: error gathering device information while adding custom device "/dev/ttyACM0": no such file or directory`.
(4) `crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3 … /dev/ttyACM0` (really `/dev/null` under another name) and `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),20(dialout)`.

**FL.12-E3:** Without the socket mount RViz exits with `qt.qpa.xcb: could not connect to display` and a Qt platform plugin error. With it, the RViz
window opens on your desktop (on Windows, as a normal window like other WSLg apps). `Global Status: Ok` may show a warning about the `map` frame
until something publishes TF, which is expected.

**FL.12-E4:** The dry run prints `docker run --rm -it -e ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0 --device /dev/ttyACM0 --group-add 20 ros:jazzy-ros-base bash`. Inside:
`crw-rw---- 1 root dialout 166, 0 … /dev/ttyACM0`, `groups=…,20(dialout)`, and Python prints bytes from the REPL such as `b'\r\n>>> '`. After a replug,
the same container fails (`[Errno 5] Input/output error` or `could not open port … No such file or directory`). With `-v /dev:/dev --device-cgroup-rule='c 166:* rmw'`
the replugged device works without restarting the container (if it came back as `ttyACM0`, so check `ls /dev/ttyACM*`).

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: `ros2 topic list` shows topics from another container or machine, but `echo` receives nothing

1. Same host, `--network host` or shared network? Add `--ipc host` to **all** ROS containers, or set `FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4`.
2. Different machines? Check the QoS match (`ros2 topic info -v /topic`), a covered topic in module 04.
3. Firewall on UDP 7400+ for unicast data ([FL.09](FL.09-networking-basics.md)).

### Symptom: a container can't see nodes on the Pi (or vice versa)

1. Is the container on the default bridge? Bridge is NAT-ed. Use `--network host` **on a native Linux host**.
2. Docker Desktop? "host" is the Docker VM. Run the laptop side natively in WSL (mirrored networking) or dual boot, and keep Docker for the Pi or for single-machine sims.
3. Same `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` inside the container? `docker exec <c> env | grep ROS_`.

### Symptom: `could not open port /dev/ttyACM0` inside the container

1. `No such file or directory`: not passed (`--device`), passed a symlink path that resolved differently, or the device was replugged after start.
2. `Permission denied`: the container user isn't in the device's group. Run `id` inside, `ls -ln /dev/ttyACM0` for the numeric GID, and `--group-add <gid>`.
3. `Operation not permitted`: the node exists but the device cgroup doesn't allow it (you bind-mounted `/dev` without a `--device-cgroup-rule`).
4. On Windows: is the device even in Linux (`usbipd attach --wsl`)? Docker Desktop containers can't use COM ports.

### Symptom: GUI app says `could not connect to display` / `Authorization required`

1. `echo $DISPLAY` inside the container: empty means you didn't pass `-e DISPLAY`.
2. `ls /tmp/.X11-unix` inside: empty means the socket isn't mounted (Docker Desktop: use the `/run/desktop/mnt/host/wslg/.X11-unix` source).
3. `Authorization required` on native Linux: `xhost +local:` on the host.
4. Opens but black or very slow: software rendering. Try `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` to confirm, then set up GPU access, or run the GUI natively.

## Common mistakes

- **`--privileged` "to make USB work"**: grants root on the host and hides the missing `--device`/group configuration.
- **`--network host` without `--ipc host`** for several ROS containers on one machine.
- **Assuming Docker Desktop's host network is your LAN.**
- **Using `osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop-full` on the Pi**: amd64 only, `exec format error`.
- **`xhost +`** (allow everyone, including the network) instead of `xhost +local:`, and never revoking it.
- **Baking the device path into the image** or relying on udev symlinks inside the container.
- **Running the dev container as root** and creating root-owned files in your bind-mounted workspace. The course image uses a UID-1000 user for this reason.
- **Different `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` inside and outside** because `-e ROS_DOMAIN_ID` was forgotten.

## Knowledge check

1. Which kernel mechanism makes `mknod` + `open` of a serial device fail inside a default container, and which error do you see?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The device cgroup, which only allows whitelisted device numbers. The open fails with `Operation not permitted`. `--device` or `--device-cgroup-rule` adds an allow rule.
   </details>

2. Two containers use `--network host`. `ros2 topic list` shows `/chatter`, but `ros2 topic echo /chatter` receives nothing. Explain and give two fixes.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Sharing the network namespace makes Fast DDS treat the peers as local and use shared memory, but their separate IPC namespaces (`/dev/shm`) can't see each
   other's segments. Discovery still works over UDP. Fixes: `--ipc host` for both, or `FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4`.
   </details>

3. Why doesn't `--network host` on Docker Desktop for Windows let the Pi discover your containerized nodes?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   On Docker Desktop, "host" is Docker Desktop's Linux VM, not the Windows machine's Wi-Fi interface. Host networking there is layer-4 only, so the
   container isn't a multicast peer on your LAN.
   </details>

4. You unplugged and replugged the Pico. The driver in the container started with `--device /dev/ttyACM0` now fails. Why, and what's the least-privilege setup that survives replugging?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   `--device` creates the node once at start, and the replug creates a new host node the container doesn't have. Use `-v /dev:/dev --device-cgroup-rule='c 166:* rmw' --group-add dialout`.
   </details>

5. Name three things `--privileged` grants that `--device /dev/ttyACM0 --group-add dialout` doesn't.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Access to all host devices (including disks), all Linux capabilities (e.g. `SYS_ADMIN` to mount filesystems, `SYS_MODULE` to load kernel modules), and
   disabled seccomp/AppArmor confinement. Together these make container escape trivial.
   </details>

6. Which image do you use on the Raspberry Pi 5 and why not the one you use on the laptop?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   `ros:jazzy-ros-base` (or `-perception`), which is multi-arch with arm64. `osrf/ros:jazzy-desktop-full` is amd64-only and includes GUI and simulation packages the Pi doesn't need.
   </details>

7. What two things must a container have to open an X11 window, and what's the Docker Desktop-specific difference?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The X11 socket (`/tmp/.X11-unix` mounted) and `DISPLAY` set. On Docker Desktop the socket source is `/run/desktop/mnt/host/wslg/.X11-unix` with `DISPLAY=:0`,
   because the containers run in Docker Desktop's VM, not your WSL distro.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Build a two-machine ROS 2 setup where **the Pi runs its driver in a container** and **the laptop visualizes**:

- On the Pi: a `compose.yaml` service from `ros:jazzy-ros-base` with `network_mode: host`, `ipc: host`, the Pico via the hotplug-safe pattern, `group_add`
  instead of privileged, `restart: unless-stopped`, and a driver node (or `ros2 topic pub` of fake odometry if module 04 isn't done yet).
- On the laptop: RViz (native WSL/Ubuntu, or a container on native Linux) shows the Pi's topic.
- `docker inspect` proves the driver container has `"Privileged": false`, `"CapAdd": null`, `"IpcMode": "host"`, and a `DeviceCgroupRules` entry for `c 166:* rmw`.
- A README with the one-line reason for each non-default flag.

Acceptance criteria: after `sudo reboot` on the Pi, the topic reappears on the laptop without manual steps. Unplugging and replugging the Pico recovers
within 10 s without restarting the container (your driver must retry opening the port, [03.03](../../03-robot-software/03.03-robust-serial-communication.md)).
Your teacher reviews every flag and agrees it's necessary.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** If the containerized driver commands real motors, put the robot on a stand with the wheels in the air for the reboot and replug tests.
> A restarting container may resume publishing the last velocity command.
